raw_text:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a life-threatening form of heart failure that affects women of childbearing age [1]. It is defined as an idiopathic cardiomyopathy presenting with left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction, characterized by an LV ejection fraction (LVEF) of less than 45%, occurring toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, when no other cause of heart failure is identified [2]. Although relatively rare, the incidence of PPCM varies significantly across geographic regions and ethnic groups, with the highest reported rates in Haiti and parts of Africa, and lower rates in Europe and North America [3]. Identified risk factors include advanced maternal age, multiparity, multiple gestations, gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, and black ancestry [4].

The complex pathophysiology of PPCM is currently conceptualized as a "two-hit" vascular-hormonal process driven by angiogenic imbalance and genetic susceptibility [5]. A pivotal pathway involves the cleaving of the hormone prolactin by the protease cathepsin D under conditions of increased oxidative stress. This cleavage generates a toxic 16-kDa prolactin fragment, which promotes endothelial cell apoptosis, impairs cardiomyocyte metabolism, and disrupts the microvasculature [6]. Additionally, the high anti-angiogenic environment of late pregnancy, characterized by elevated levels of soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1)—especially in patients with concomitant preeclampsia—further compromises myocardial perfusion and function [7]. On a genetic level, up to 15% of patients carry truncating mutations in the titin gene (*TTN*), showing a strong genetic overlap with dilated cardiomyopathy [8, 9]. Mutations in other genes, such as *BAG3*, *DSP*, and *MYH7*, have also been identified, underscoring the role of a pre-existing genetic vulnerability that is unmasked by the hemodynamic and metabolic stresses of pregnancy [10].

Clinical presentation of PPCM varies widely, ranging from mild dyspnea to severe cardiogenic shock [11]. Because early symptoms—such as fatigue, dyspnea, and peripheral edema—mimic the physiological changes of late pregnancy and the early postpartum period, the diagnosis of PPCM is frequently delayed, leading to worse clinical outcomes [12]. Echocardiography remains the diagnostic gold standard, demonstrating an LVEF <45%, often accompanied by LV dilation [13]. Elevated cardiac biomarkers, particularly N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), are essential for both screening and monitoring [14]. Electrocardiographic abnormalities are highly common but non-specific, frequently showing sinus tachycardia, ST-segment changes, or T-wave inversions [15, 16].

The clinical management of PPCM requires a multidisciplinary cardio-obstetric approach, with strategies tailored to whether the patient is pre- or postpartum [17]. During pregnancy, standard heart failure drugs that interfere with the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), such as angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs), and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs), are strictly contraindicated due to the risk of fetotoxicity [18]. Instead, hydralazine, nitrates, and beta-blockers (such as metoprolol succinate) are utilized [19]. Postpartum, standard guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) including ARNIs, beta-blockers, MRAs, and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors must be promptly initiated and optimized [20]. Due to the high risk of thromboembolism associated with the hypercoagulable state of the postpartum period and severe LV dysfunction, anticoagulation is recommended for patients with an LVEF <35% [21].

A disease-specific treatment option is the use of bromocriptine, a dopamine D2 receptor agonist that blocks pituitary prolactin release [22]. Registry and randomized trial data, including the German multicenter trial, have demonstrated that adding bromocriptine to standard GDMT improves LVEF recovery and clinical outcomes [23, 24]. In patients presenting with acute cardiogenic shock, advanced mechanical circulatory support, such as extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) or a left ventricular assist device (LVAD), may serve as a bridge to recovery or transplantation [25, 26].

While PPCM is associated with significant morbidity, it carries a higher rate of myocardial recovery compared to other forms of non-ischemic cardiomyopathy [27]. Up to 50–70% of women show substantial recovery of LV function, typically within 6 to 12 months after diagnosis [28]. Important predictors of poor recovery include an initial LVEF <30%, severe LV dilation, and black race [29]. For women who plan subsequent pregnancies, comprehensive counseling is critical. A subsequent pregnancy carries a substantial risk of relapse (around 20%), even in women who have fully recovered their LV function, while those with persistent LV dysfunction face extremely high rates of clinical deterioration, heart failure recurrence, and maternal mortality [30].
